intended_object: The docstring describes the ideal of leading coefficients of an ideal I ⊆ R[X]: the set {lc(p) : p ∈ I} ⊆ R, which is an ideal and contains 0 because 0 ∈ I. This ideal is the standard ingredient in the proof of Hilbert's basis theorem.
explanation:
`leadingCoeffNth I n` is the image of {p ∈ I : deg p ≤ n} under the linear map p ↦ coeff p n. In other words, it is the set of degree-n coefficients of the polynomials in I of degree at most n. That is exactly the set of leading coefficients of degree-n elements of I, together with 0.

The definition takes the supremum of these ideals over all n. Because I is closed under left multiplication by X, which is central, the family is increasing in n: if p ∈ I has degree ≤ n, then X·p ∈ I has degree ≤ n+1 and the same coefficient in degree n+1. The supremum of an increasing chain of ideals is their union. So the result is {lc(p) : p ∈ I} ∪ {0}, the textbook ideal of leading coefficients.

The setting is natural. A semiring is the most general hypothesis under which polynomial rings and ideals make sense, and for a noncommutative R, `Ideal` means a left ideal, which is consistent with how the construction works. I found no separate, more general version of this notion elsewhere in Mathlib.
